premises and conclusion systematically. The argument is represented as follows: the
conjunction ~A · ~B is true only when both A and B are false, while the disjunction (A ∨

but the conclusion C does not follow since it is not a definitive consequence of the
premises. Thus, the argument is invalid.

In his article "Will Cloning Harm People?", Pence employs Kant's humanity formulation to
argue that cloning is morally acceptable by emphasizing the intrinsic worth and dignity of
all human beings. According to Kant, individuals should be treated as ends in themselves
and not merely as means to an end. Pence contends that cloning, when conducted ethically,
can enhance human welfare by providing solutions to infertility and genetic diseases, thus
respecting the autonomy and value of potential individuals. By framing cloning as a means
to promote human well-being, Pence aligns with Kantian ethics, suggesting that the act of
cloning can be justified if it acknowledges and preserves the humanity of the cloned
individuals. Ultimately, this application of Kant's formulation positions cloning as a
morally viable option that upholds human dignity rather than undermining it.
